text: 16. Source Code Change Impact Matrix

This section is the **change-impact reference** for the CoLab codebase. Its purpose is operational: before anyone modifies a folder, they should be able to look it up here and immediately understand five things — what that code controls, what visibly breaks if it is changed wrongly, what tests must pass before the change ships, what it depends on, and how dangerous a mistake would be. It is written for a future engineer who has never met the original author and who is touching this code under deadline pressure. Treat every **Critical** and **High** row as a stop-and-think gate, not a formality.

In plain terms: CoLab is one large single-page frontend (`frontend/app/src`) talking to one Express backend (`backend/app/src`) over REST and Socket.IO, persisting to a single MySQL database (`database/`), with real-time audio and video carried by a self-hosted LiveKit SFU and a coturn TURN relay (`infrastructure/`). The whole thing is wired together by a handful of load-bearing files. A surprising amount of risk is concentrated in a small number of god-files and config files: `CoLabV1.tsx` (9,039 lines), `v1.css` (16,672 lines), the migration runner, the auth middleware, and the LiveKit / coturn / nginx triad. The matrix below is ordered roughly from frontend to infrastructure, and the prose after it goes deep on the three areas where a bad change does the most damage: **calls/media, database migrations, and authentication**.

title: How to read the Risk column
text: Low = a mistake is cosmetic or self-contained and caught in review. Medium = a mistake degrades one module for some users. High = a mistake breaks a core product surface (messaging, calls, login) for many users but is recoverable by redeploy. Critical = a mistake can cause data loss, lock every user out, or take the whole platform down, and may not be trivially reversible.
16.1 The Change Impact Matrix

The table covers every folder and file the handbook is required to document. Line counts and behaviours below were verified against the live tree (for example `CoLabV1.tsx` = 9,039 lines, `v1.css` = 16,672 lines, `ChatView.tsx` = 6,296 lines, `MeetingStage.tsx` = 2,850 lines, and `database/migrations` contains 47 files `0001`–`0047`).

rows: `frontend/app/src/components/CoLabV1.tsx`

The god-component (9,039 lines). Owns nearly all app state (mode, theme, conversations, activeId, settings, modals, toasts, nav history), the `mode` view switch (chats, dashboard, calls, tasks, etc.), auth/token bootstrap, socket wiring + reconnect resync, the 1:1 / group `CallModal` and incoming-ring UI, and `applySettings()` (theme/accent/density/zoom body classes).

Everything. A bad edit can blank the entire SPA (it is the only thing `app/page.tsx` renders), drop socket reconnection resync (lost messages/badges after a network blip), break login/logout, or break 1:1 calls. The inline `ActivityView` and `DashboardView` live here too.

Full smoke of every `mode` view; login + signup + logout; 1:1 call connect/accept/hangup; socket disconnect→reconnect resync; theme/accent/zoom toggles via `applySettings`. Run `tsc` (build is gated on it).
`lib/api.ts`, `lib/socket.ts`, `lib/config.ts`, `lib/logger.ts`, `lib/callDiagnostics.ts`, `lib/sounds.ts`, all view components, `livekit-client`.
Critical
`frontend/app/src/components/MeetingStage.tsx`

Full meeting room UI (2,850 lines): LiveKit `Room` lifecycle, participant tiles, host controls (mute-all, per-participant mute/eject, promote/demote, lobby admit/deny), in-meeting chat + reactions + hand-raise, screen share, and the meeting `Room` options (1.7 Mbit/s cap). Its `.ms-*` CSS classes are reused by the 1:1/group call modal in `CoLabV1`.

All scheduled meetings: video may not render, host controls become no-ops, lobby/lock gating can silently fail, screen share breaks. Because `.ms-*` classes are shared, a styling change here can also distort the 1:1 call modal.

Schedule + join a meeting (host and guest); lobby admit/deny; mute-all + eject; hand-raise; screen share (with + without system audio); 2+ remote tiles render (regression: deprecated `room.participants` must stay `room.remoteParticipants`). `tsc`.
`livekit-client`, `lib/callDiagnostics.ts`, `CallDebugPanel.tsx`, `MeetingRoom.tsx`, backend `/api/meetings/*` + `/api/calls/token`.
High
`frontend/app/src/lib/api.ts`

Single `api` object (683 lines, ~150 methods) — every REST call goes through the `req()` helper. Owns the `{ok,data,error}` envelope contract, attaches the Bearer token, surfaces `err.status` (callers key off 403 for call/meeting denial), re-validates via `/api/auth/me` before dispatching `colab:unauthorized` on a 401, and does XHR upload-with-progress + raw-blob voicemail/recording uploads.

Every network feature. A wrong base URL or envelope change breaks all data loading; a regression in the 401 logic either logs users out on transient blips or fails to log them out when truly unauthorized. Upload progress / voicemail bodies are easy to break (raw vs JSON).
Exercise representative reads/writes across modules; confirm 401 path re-checks `/auth/me`; file upload progress; voicemail blob upload; `tsc`.
`lib/config.ts` (base URL), browser `fetch`/`XMLHttpRequest`, backend `/api/*`.
High
`frontend/app/src/lib/socket.ts`

Socket.IO client bootstrap: `connectSocket(token)` with same-origin URL, `auth:{token}`, **polling-first** transports + `tryAllTransports` (Next dev proxy can't carry a raw WS upgrade), `reconnection:true`, and the `EVENTS` map (~60 named events) that must stay byte-aligned with `shared/src/events.ts`.

Realtime stops: no live messages/typing/presence/calls. If the `EVENTS` map drifts from the backend/shared contract, events silently no-op (the worst kind of bug — looks connected, nothing arrives). Wrong transport order can stop connections behind the Next dev proxy.
Realtime message echo; typing; presence; incoming-call ring; reconnect after network drop. Diff `EVENTS` against `shared/src/events.ts`. `tsc`.
`socket.io-client`, `lib/config.ts`, `shared/src/events.ts` contract, Next `/socket.io` rewrite.
High
`frontend/app/src/lib/callDiagnostics.ts`

WebRTC observability (additive, no behaviour change): polls `peerConnection.getStats()` every 1.5 s; tracks ICE state, selected candidate-pair type (host/srflx/relay), udp/tcp, `turnUsed`, `turnAdvertised`, RTT, loss, kbps; emits grep-able `[CALLDIAG]` lines and powers `CallDebugPanel`.

Low product impact — it only observes. But if it throws inside the stats loop it can disrupt the call UI in `CoLabV1`/`MeetingStage` that call it. Losing it removes the main tool for diagnosing 'call connected but no media' in the field.
Confirm a call still connects with diagnostics on; panel opens via `?calldebug=1` / `localStorage colab_call_debug=1`; no thrown errors in the 1.5 s poll. `tsc`.
Browser WebRTC `getStats`, consumed by `CoLabV1` + `MeetingStage`, surfaced in `CallDebugPanel.tsx`.
Low
`frontend/app/src/lib/logger.ts`

Zero-dep structured logger: 400-entry ring buffer, pub/sub (`subscribeLogs`), levels + categories, plain-English hint per HTTP status, mirrors to console, exposes `window.colabLogs`, and `initGlobalLogging()` captures window error/online/offline. Feeds `DiagnosticsPanel`.
Observability only — product features keep working. A regression degrades the `DiagnosticsPanel` health chips and the copyable bug report, making field support harder. Low blast radius.
Open `DiagnosticsPanel` (Ctrl+Alt+D / `?diag=1`); confirm health chips + copy-report; force an error and see the hint. `tsc`.
None beyond the browser; consumed by `DiagnosticsPanel.tsx`.
Low
`frontend/app/src/styles/v1.css`

The ENTIRE design system in one 16,672-line stylesheet: CSS-custom-property tokens (`--g50..--g900`, accent, surfaces, radii, shadows), every theme (light/dark/oled/midnight/slate/forest) via `body` class overrides, the auto large-display `zoom` ramp (1.15→4 across 2100→7680 px), all responsive breakpoints, ambient `amb-borealis`, and the shared `.ms-*` call/meeting styling.

Visual regressions anywhere — themes, contrast, layout, clipping, 4K/8K scaling, call/meeting chrome. A single mis-scoped selector (e.g. an OLED override leaking to light) degrades a whole theme; touching `.ms-*` hits both meetings and 1:1 calls.
Visual pass across all 6 themes + auto; density + zoom levels; mobile breakpoints (320→3440 px, zero horizontal overflow per `responsive.spec.ts`); call/meeting chrome unchanged.
Consumed by `layout.tsx` import and every component; Google Fonts.
Medium
`backend/app/src/routes`

Thin HTTP controllers (21 route modules) mounted under `/api` in `app.ts`: auth, conversations/messaging, calls, meetings, files, users, tasks, reminders, notifications, invites, search, ai, e2ee, audit, bookmarks, link-preview, public (no-auth), livekit webhook, debug (non-prod). They parse input, call services, and emit socket events via `req.app.get('io')`.

The specific API surface touched. Removing a `router.use(authMiddleware)` exposes a private resource (auth-bypass). Breaking raw-body routes (`/files`, `/calls/voicemail`, `/meetings/:id/recordings/upload`, `/livekit/webhook`) corrupts uploads/recordings. Wrong membership gate = IDOR.
Per-route auth gate present; happy-path + 403 denial; raw-body upload routes still buffer correctly; socket emit still fires. Backend `tsc`.
`middleware/auth.ts`, `middleware/rateLimit.ts`, `services/*`, `asyncRouter.ts`, `shared/src/http` envelope, Socket.IO.
High
`backend/app/src/services`

All business logic (~24 service modules): `authService` (scrypt + JWT), `messageService` (send/history/edit/react/pin with `assertMember` 403 gate + DM block enforcement), `meetingService` (lobby/lock/eject), `livekitService` (token mint + host controls), `callService`, `fileService`+`storageService`, `notificationService`, `scheduledMessageService`, `tokenBlocklist`, `credentialPolicy`, etc. Routes are thin; this is where the rules live.

The actual product behaviour and its security. A bug in `messageService.assertMember` or `meetingService.enterRoom` is an authorization hole. A bug in `authService` breaks login or token verification. A bug in `livekitService.roomToken` breaks all media.
Service-level unit/integration of the touched rule; membership/role denial paths; for auth/token/livekit changes, full login + call regression. Backend `tsc`.
`platform.ts`/`getDb` (MySQL), `livekit-server-sdk`, `jsonwebtoken`, Redis (optional), `config/src`.
Critical
Backend socket layer (`backend/app/src/realtime/socket.ts`)

`attachRealtime(httpServer)`: Socket.IO server, optional Redis adapter behind a 3 s readiness race (must finish before any room join), handshake auth (`authService.verify`), per-user `user:<uid>` rooms + `conv:<cid>` + `meeting:<mid>`, the full 1:1 call lifecycle (request/accept/decline/cancel/hangup + no-answer timers), group huddles, meeting interactions, presence fan-out, and the per-user MESSAGE_SEND token bucket (cap 20, refill 5/s).

Realtime + calls. The classic prod failure: swapping the Redis adapter AFTER sockets join rooms makes `io.to(userRoom)` silently stop delivering — incoming-call rings and notifications vanish. Breaking the disconnect sweep leaves ghost huddle participants and stale ringing calls.
Two-client realtime (message echo, typing, presence); incoming-call ring across tabs; huddle join/leave cleanup on tab-close; reconnect; with Redis adapter on AND off. Backend `tsc`.
`authService`, `huddleStore` (Redis or in-proc), `@socket.io/redis-adapter`, `shared/src/events.ts`, all emitting routes.
Critical
`database/migrations`

47 ordered `.sql` files (`0001`–`0047`) — the authoritative schema DDL, applied at boot by the statement-level idempotent runner in `database/src/bootstrap.ts`, tracked in `schema_migrations`. Defines every table, index, FK, trigger (append-only `audit_log`, reject-past-meeting), the soft-delete trio (0046), and `dm_key` uniqueness.

Persistence and data integrity. A non-idempotent or destructive statement can crash the boot migration loop or, worse, drop/alter live data. Out-of-order numbering breaks the ledger. A wrong FK `ON DELETE` rule can cascade-delete unexpectedly.

Apply against a copy of prod data, not just an empty DB; re-run twice to confirm idempotency; verify `schema_migrations` ledger; back up before applying. Boot the backend and confirm the migrate loop completes.
`database/src/bootstrap.ts` runner, `database/src/migrate.ts`, MySQL 8/InnoDB.
Critical
`infrastructure/livekit`

SFU config per environment: `livekit.yaml` (local), `.live.yaml`, `.test.yaml`, `.mumbai.yaml`, `.prod.yaml`. Controls signalling port 7534, ICE udp 7532 / tcp 7531, built-in TURN udp 7533, `use_external_ip`, `node_ip`, and (local/mumbai) the Egress webhook + room-state Redis.

All audio/video. `use_external_ip:false` on the live box advertises only the private `10.200.3.17` candidate → off-network calls hang (the exact bug fixed by setting it `true`). Wrong ports/node_ip = no media path. Keys here are overridden at runtime by `LIVEKIT_KEYS` env.

After any change: `docker logs colab-livekit | grep -i candidate` shows BOTH the private and public IP; on-network call works; off-network (4G) call works; `[CALLDIAG]` shows a connected candidate pair.
coturn (fallback relay), nginx `/livekit` proxy (strips prefix), `livekit-server-sdk` token mint, GCP firewall (udp:7532/tcp:7531).
Critical
`infrastructure/coturn`

`turnserver.conf` for the TURN relay: static long-term credential (`lt-cred-mech`, literal `user=collab-turn:<password>`, realm `collab.resulticks.com`), listeners 3478 (plain) / 5349 (TLS) / 443 (alt-TLS, the only port that reliably traverses locked-down mobile/corporate NAT), relay range 49152–49251, TLS certs, and the `allowed-peer-ip` whitelist for the SFUs (open-relay/SSRF guard).

Calls on the strictest NATs (mobile/corporate/hotel). The credential MUST match `.env.live TURN_USERNAME`/`TURN_PASSWORD` byte-for-byte — a one-character drift means the browser can't authenticate to the relay and locked-down clients can't connect. Removing the `allowed-peer-ip` SFU entries blocks the relay→SFU hop; widening it risks an open relay.
On a network that needs TURN (mobile data, no UDP), a call connects with `turnUsed=true` in `[CALLDIAG]`; credential matches `.env.live`; `allowed-peer-ip` still lists the live SFU `10.200.3.17`.
`.env.live` TURN creds, TLS certs (`fullchain.pem`/`privkey.key`), the LiveKit SFU it relays to.
High
`infrastructure/nginx`

`nginx.conf`: reverse proxy on port 7530, `client_max_body_size 100M`. Routes `/api/` and `/socket.io/` (with WS upgrade) to backend, `/livekit` to `livekit:7534` with `rewrite ^/livekit/?(.*)$ /$1 break` to STRIP the prefix (LiveKit serves at `/rtc`) + 86400 s timeout, `/minio/` to MinIO console, `/` to frontend. Maps `X-Forwarded-Proto` (default https) so the backend builds correct `wss://` URLs.

User-facing routing. Dropping the `/livekit` prefix-strip → LiveKit 404 on `/livekit/rtc/v1/validate` → call media fails. Losing the WS upgrade headers on `/socket.io/` or `/livekit` breaks realtime and signalling. A wrong `X-Forwarded-Proto` yields mixed-content `ws://` and broken calls.
Load the app through nginx; messages flow (socket.io upgrade); a call connects (signalling reaches LiveKit, no 404); body up to 100 MB uploads; `X-Forwarded-Proto` arrives as https at the backend.
frontend:3000, backend:4000, livekit:7534, minio:9000; corporate LB terminating TLS upstream.
High
`docker-compose.live.yml`

The LIVE topology for collab.resulticks.com / 10.200.3.17. Publishes ONLY two host surfaces — nginx `${NGINX_PORT:-7524}:7530` and LiveKit media (7531/tcp, 7532/udp, 7533/udp); db/backend/frontend/minio/livekit-7534 stay internal. Sets `DB_PROFILE` (default `local`), `COLAB_FRESH_START`, and profile-gates coturn OFF (it runs on a separate public box).

Production wiring. Publishing the wrong ports causes host collisions on the shared box. Setting `DB_PROFILE` wrong points the live app at the wrong database. A `down -v` here deletes the MySQL volume = total data loss. coturn accidentally enabled clashes with nginx on :443.
Bring the stack up on a staging box; confirm only nginx+media are exposed; backend connects to the intended DB profile; back up the volume first; never `down -v`.
`.env.live`, all service images, the host's firewall rules, `database/dumps/colab_full.sql` (first-boot import).
Critical
`.env.live`

The filled secret + config file for the live deploy: `AUTH_JWT_SECRET`, `LIVEKIT_API_KEY/_SECRET`, `TURN_USERNAME/_PASSWORD` (must match coturn conf), `DATABASE_URL_LIVE` + `DB_PROFILE`, S3/MinIO creds, `REDIS_URL`, feature flags. The production boot guard refuses to start on bundled-default secrets.

Boot and security. A weak/default `AUTH_JWT_SECRET` or `LIVEKIT_API_SECRET` either fails the boot guard (won't start) or, if it slipped through, lets anyone forge JWTs / LiveKit tokens. A TURN password drift from coturn conf silently kills relayed calls. A wrong `DATABASE_URL` writes to the wrong DB.
Boot guard passes with real (non-default) secrets; TURN creds equal `turnserver.conf` byte-for-byte; `DB_PROFILE`→`DATABASE_URL_LIVE` resolves to the intended DB; calls + login work end-to-end.
Consumed by `config/src/index.ts`, every backend service, coturn, the boot secret guard.
Critical

text: 16.2 Architecture at a Glance (what a change ripples through)

Before drilling into the high-risk areas, it helps to see how a single change propagates. The runtime is a layered stack: a same-origin browser SPA, a reverse proxy that keeps everything same-origin, the Express API + Socket.IO, and the data/media plane.

title: Runtime layers a change can ripple through

text: The key insight for change-impact reasoning: the **event-name contract** (`shared/src/events.ts`) and the **REST envelope** (`{ok,data,error}`) are the two seams that the frontend and backend must agree on. Most 'it compiles but nothing happens' bugs come from one side of one of those seams drifting. The second insight is that the **media plane is physically separate** from the app plane — signalling rides the same nginx that serves the app, but RTP/ICE media goes straight to the LiveKit box's published ports (7531/7532/7533) and, for hard NATs, to the coturn relay. That separation is why a perfectly working chat app can still have totally broken calls, and vice-versa.
16.3 Deep Dive — Calls & Media (highest operational risk)

**Plain language:** calls and meetings are the part of CoLab most likely to 'work on my machine' and fail in the field, because they depend on the public internet's NAT/firewall reality, not just on application code. The app code for calls is largely correct and hardened; the failures are almost always in the **media plane** — the path the actual audio/video packets take.

**Engineering language:** CoLab uses a LiveKit SFU (Selective Forwarding Unit), not peer-to-peer. Every participant publishes to the SFU and subscribes from it (`client → SFU → client`). The browser learns where the SFU is from ICE candidates the SFU advertises, and learns about the fallback TURN relay from the `iceServers` array embedded in the room-token response (`livekitService.roomToken`). The room token is minted server-side with a per-join identity `userId__<uuid>` (so an honest page reload does not trip `DUPLICATE_IDENTITY`; that only fires on a genuine second tab/device), gated by membership in `routes/calls.ts POST /token`: a `callId` must match `call.initiatorId` or `call.peerId` (a 403 IDOR guard, verified at lines 112–116), a `conversationId` must pass `db.conversations.isMember`, and a `meetingId` is gated by `meetingService.enterRoom`, which enforces eject → lock → lobby in that order.

**The single most important media fact in this codebase:** on the live box, `infrastructure/livekit/livekit.live.yaml` sets `use_external_ip: true` with `node_ip` left UNSET. This is deliberate and was established by live debugging. The box has both a private corporate NIC (`10.200.3.17`) and a 1:1-NAT public IP. With `use_external_ip:true` and `node_ip` unset, LiveKit advertises BOTH candidates — internal/VPN clients pair on `10.200.3.17` (no hairpin), and off-network clients (home, 4G) pair on the STUN-discovered public IP. With `use_external_ip:false` it advertised only the private candidate, so off-network clients had no reachable SFU candidate and calls hung with `turnUsed=false`. **Do not 'simplify' this back to false, and do not pin `node_ip`.**

title: Do not revert use_external_ip
text: Setting `use_external_ip:false` or pinning `node_ip` on the live SFU is the recurring footgun that silently breaks every off-network call while on-network calls keep working — making it look like an app bug. After any LiveKit config change, run `docker logs colab-livekit | grep -i candidate` and confirm BOTH 10.200.3.17 AND the public IP appear.

**The TURN relay** (`infrastructure/coturn/turnserver.conf`) is the fallback for the strictest NATs (mobile data, corporate, hotel). It uses static long-term credentials (`lt-cred-mech`, a literal `user=collab-turn:<password>` line, NOT HMAC/`use-auth-secret`), so the backend sends `TURN_USERNAME`/`TURN_PASSWORD` verbatim in the token's `iceServers`. These MUST match `.env.live` byte-for-byte — a single drifted character means locked-down clients fail to authenticate to the relay and their calls hang while everyone else is fine. The relay listens on 3478 (plain), 5349 (TLS), and 443 (alt-TLS — the only transport that reliably crosses locked-down NAT). The `allowed-peer-ip` whitelist (live SFU `10.200.3.17`, test SFU `10.205.11.8`) lets the relay reach the SFUs while all RFC1918/bogon ranges are denied to prevent open-relay/SSRF abuse.

**The signalling vs media split** is the other classic confusion. Signalling (the WebSocket that negotiates the call) flows through nginx at `/livekit`, which MUST strip the prefix (`rewrite ^/livekit/?(.*)$ /$1 break`) because LiveKit serves at `/rtc`. If that rewrite is removed, LiveKit returns 404 on `/livekit/rtc/v1/validate` and the call's media connection never establishes — but the symptom looks like a media failure, not a routing one. Media itself (RTP/ICE) does not go through nginx at all; it goes straight to the box's published 7532/udp + 7531/tcp ports, which is why GCP ingress on those ports is a one-time IT requirement.

**Failure scenarios and triage, in order:** (1) 'Unable to reach media server' immediately → containers not running; run `docker ps` first. (2) On-network calls work, off-network hang → `use_external_ip`/firewall on the SFU box (check the candidate log). (3) Only the strictest NATs fail → TURN credential drift or coturn not reachable on 443; check `[CALLDIAG]` for `turnAdvertised` vs `turnUsed`. (4) Call connects then no audio/video → check the candidate-pair type and whether the `/livekit` prefix strip is intact. (5) Latency ~200–300 ms even in-room → physics, not a bug: the SFU is in us-east and users are in India; the Mumbai regional-media kit (`docker-compose.mumbai.yml`) relocates only the media engine to asia-south1, no app code change.

**Testing required for any calls/media change:** a 1:1 call (connect/accept/hangup), a group call with host controls, a meeting with lobby/lock, screen share with and without system audio, and — non-negotiably — at least one off-network test on real mobile data, watching `[CALLDIAG]` for the selected candidate pair. **Business impact:** calls and meetings are the CEO-demo top priority; a silent media regression reads as 'the product doesn't work' even when chat, files, and everything else are perfect.
16.4 Deep Dive — Database Migrations (highest data risk)

**Plain language:** migrations are the only code in CoLab that can permanently destroy customer data. Everything else is recoverable by redeploying the previous build; a bad migration is not. They run automatically on every backend boot, against the live database, with no human in the loop. That combination is why this is a Critical row.

**Engineering language:** `database/src/bootstrap.ts` `migrate()` tracks applied files in `schema_migrations(filename PK, applied_at)` and applies each unseen `.sql` file STATEMENT-BY-STATEMENT via a `BEGIN/END`-aware `splitSqlStatements()` (so a `CREATE TRIGGER` body doesn't split on its internal semicolons). It is idempotent by design: it swallows the 'already applied' MySQL errnos — 1050 (table exists), 1060 (dup column), 1061 (dup key), 1826 (dup FK), 1359 (trigger exists), 1304 (proc exists), 1065 (empty fragment) — and skips `CREATE TRIGGER` when the DB user is non-SUPER (errno 1419), since those rules are also app-enforced. Real errors re-throw, and because it is statement-level, a retry resumes from the failure point instead of crash-looping. This idempotent runner is the reason a half-applied migration no longer wedges every boot.

steps.label: Apply statement
steps.detail: swallow idempotent errnos; re-throw real errors

text: **Rules a migration author must follow (each one is a real footgun):** number the file strictly after the current max (`0048_…` next); make every statement idempotent or guarded; never write a destructive statement (`DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, data-losing `ALTER`) into an auto-run migration; respect the soft-delete convention (migration 0046 added the uniform `deleted/deleted_at/deleted_by` trio to 24 tables with `DEFAULT 0` so it is behaviour-neutral — prefer a soft delete over a hard one); and be careful with FK `ON DELETE` semantics, because a wrong `CASCADE` can quietly chain-delete rows. The `audit_log` table is append-only, enforced at the DB by triggers (`SIGNAL 45000` on UPDATE/DELETE) — do not try to mutate it.

title: Never run down -v; always back up first
text: `docker compose down -v` deletes the `colab_mysqldata` volume = total data loss. Use `down` or `up -d --build`. Before any deploy that includes a migration: `docker exec colab-db mysqldump -u colab -pcolab --single-transaction --routines --triggers colab > backup_<stamp>.sql`. The `initdb/*.sql` seed only runs on an EMPTY volume, so it will not re-run on an existing DB — but a fresh volume on the wrong box will start empty.

**Failure scenarios:** a non-idempotent statement that isn't in the swallowed-errno set re-throws on the second boot and blocks startup (recoverable: make it idempotent and redeploy). A destructive `ALTER` that drops a column's data is NOT recoverable without the backup. An out-of-order or renamed file confuses the ledger and may re-run or skip. **Testing required:** apply the migration against a restored copy of production data (not an empty schema), run the backend boot twice to prove idempotency, confirm the `schema_migrations` ledger has the new row exactly once, and verify dependent queries still work. **Business impact:** a data-loss migration on the live box wipes office signups that live only in that container's volume — there is no second copy unless someone took the backup.
16.5 Deep Dive — Authentication (highest blast radius)

**Plain language:** auth is the gate every request passes through. A mistake here either locks every user out (no one can log in) or, worse, lets the wrong people in (a security breach). It is a small amount of code with a platform-wide blast radius.

**Engineering language:** passwords are hashed with Node's built-in `scrypt` and stored as `saltHex:hashHex` (16-byte salt, 64-byte key); verification recomputes with the stored salt and compares via `crypto.timingSafeEqual` (constant-time). Login/signup mint a JSON Web Token (`jsonwebtoken`, HS256) with payload `{sub:userId, name}`, signed with `config.auth.jwtSecret`. **Correction to a common misconception:** the session JWT default TTL is `7d` (env `AUTH_TOKEN_TTL`), NOT 1 hour — the ~1h/3600 s TTL belongs to the SEPARATE LiveKit room token (`config.livekit.tokenTtlSec`). There is no refresh-token flow; a single long-lived access JWT is issued and stored client-side (`localStorage clb_token`), and on expiry the user re-authenticates (the frontend auto-logs-out on a confirmed 401).

`middleware/auth.ts` is the chokepoint (verified): it reads `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, calls `authService.verify`, then checks `tokenBlocklist.isBlocked(token)`, and on either failure returns 401. Logout and account-delete add the token's signature segment to the blocklist (Redis when `REDIS_URL` is set, else an in-memory Map swept every 60 s) — this is how a stateless JWT gets revocation. The Redis init is hardened with `reconnectStrategy:false` + a 3.5 s connect race so a down Redis falls back to memory rather than hanging every authed request (because `isBlocked` runs on every request).

title: Two auth landmines
text: (1) Removing or mis-ordering the `tokenBlocklist.isBlocked` check means revoked/logged-out tokens keep working until natural expiry (up to 7 days). (2) The Socket.IO handshake verifies the JWT but does NOT re-check the blocklist — only the HTTP middleware does. Do not assume socket connections are revocable mid-session the way HTTP requests are.

**The production secret guard** (in `index.ts`) refuses to boot if `AUTH_JWT_SECRET` is a bundled default or under 32 chars, or if `LIVEKIT_API_SECRET` is the default. This is the safety net that stops a forgeable-token deploy — never weaken it, and never set a default-looking secret in `.env.live`. **Signup policy** is server-side authority in `credentialPolicy.ts` (email shape + ~70 disposable-domain block; password min 9 with mixed classes + ~60 common-password reject); the frontend `passwordPolicy.ts` is a non-authoritative UX mirror and must not be treated as the gate.

**Failure scenarios:** a wrong/rotated `AUTH_JWT_SECRET` invalidates every existing token (mass logout) — recoverable by re-login but disruptive. A broken `verify` or middleware order is an instant platform-wide lockout. A weakened secret guard or a leaked secret is a forgery breach. **Testing required for any auth change:** signup, login, `GET /me`, logout (and confirm the blocklisted token is then rejected), account-delete, a deliberately expired/invalid token returns 401, the socket handshake still authenticates, and the production boot guard still fails fast on a default secret. **Business impact:** auth is binary — it works for everyone or for no one; there is no graceful degradation, so it gets the most conservative change discipline in the codebase.
16.6 Cross-Cutting Change-Discipline Rules

items.text: **Holistic fixes across all contexts.** A message-layer change must be verified for DMs, groups, AND channels (all share `conversations`/`messages` by `kind`); a call change for 1:1, group, AND meetings. Per-site patches read as 'for name's sake' — prefer a shared source plus a repo-wide grep.
items: Message previews must ALWAYS go through `lib/messageText.ts` (`messagePreview`/`messageRowPreview`); only the bubble renders sanitized HTML.

items.text: **The event-name and envelope seams are contracts.** Any change to a Socket.IO event must be mirrored across `shared/src/events.ts`, the backend `socket.ts`, and the frontend `lib/socket.ts` EVENTS map; any change to the REST shape must keep the `{ok,data,error}` envelope intact.

**Feature flags hide, they do not delete.** Search, Agents, and AI-summarize are built but gated off (`NEXT_PUBLIC_FEATURE_*`). Reactivation is flipping an env var, not re-implementing — do not delete the hidden components/routes/APIs.

**Honest maturity.** `agents/` is a scaffold whose methods throw `not implemented (Sprint 6)`; the `mcp/` server is built but unwired into any running deployment; server-side Egress recording is coded but depends on an infra container; custom status text/emoji does not exist (only manual away/busy/DND). Do not document these as live.
**The build is gated on `tsc`.** ESLint is `ignoreDuringBuilds`, but a type error fails the build — run the TypeScript check before claiming a change is done.
**Settings whitelist gotcha.** A frontend setting that isn't in the backend `DEFAULTS` is silently dropped on save; add new settings on BOTH sides.

title: The one-line rule of thumb
text: If your change touches CoLabV1.tsx, a service, the socket layer, a migration, the LiveKit/coturn/nginx triad, or .env.live — slow down, back up, and test across contexts. If it touches a single view component, a lib helper, or v1.css scoping — review carefully but it is recoverable. Everything in the Critical and High rows above can take down a core surface for many users at once.
